title: Commanders of Attention 2: The Magnetizers
hook: A half-filled scorecard clipped to a lanyard can hold attention longer than a slogan.
counterintuition: You might assume getting attention is the hard part. Instead, the harder work is keeping it, and people stay with cues that feel personal, unfinished, or unanswered.
tryThisNow: Before your next request, move one cue: the first object, first number, first place, or first shared action. Make it serve the real decision.
keyTakeaway: People rarely meet an ask in neutral air, so prepare the first cue, place, or shared action to support clear judgment before you rely on better wording.

breakdown.fastRead:
At 8:10 a.m., a person sees a half-filled scorecard clipped to a lanyard before the ask. The ask lands in a mind that is already tilted. The request walks into a room that is already leaning toward self-relevance,. Put one true cue in view first. Then ask in plain words. The cue should help them see the choice, not push them past it. If the cue adds fear or haze, change it.

Use the setup with care. Ask what they will see, hear, or touch first. If that thing helps them weigh the facts, keep it. If it pulls them toward fear, pride, haste, or fog, move it before you ask.
breakdown.deepRead:
At 2:25 p.m., picture a supervisor pausing before a hard request. The words are ready, but the room is not. A phone buzzes, a chair scrapes, and the first object in view is already telling people what kind of moment this is. The first cue does not win by force; it changes what feels worth checking.

A cue works because the mind does not wait for the full argument. It grabs what is near, vivid, repeated, personal, or shared, then uses that cue to judge what follows. That can help a good case. It can also make a weak case feel stronger than it is. The useful test is whether the cue points toward the facts people need or away from them.

Picture a client walking in with wet shoes and five spare minutes. The slide deck may be sound, but the first thing she sees may be a late fee, a crowded room, or a proud award wall that has nothing to do with her problem. Change that first sight. Put the broken part, the fair price range, the patient note, or the shared task where her eyes will go.

Try the move in a live setting. Before asking, name what the listener is likely to notice first. If that first notice helps them judge well, keep it. If it pulls them toward fear, vanity, hurry, or false comfort, change the setting. Use the setup to help people see the real choice, not to hide it.
breakdown.fullRead:
At 7:42 a.m., a team gathers around a table with coffee rings, open laptops, and one object no one can ignore: a half-filled scorecard clipped to a lanyard. Before the leader speaks, the object has done some of the work. It has told the room where to look. It has made one concern feel near and another feel far away. That is why self-relevance, unfinished gaps, and mystery hold attention after they catch it.

A mind under pressure does not sort every fact from scratch. It uses cues. A first number becomes a comparison. A trusted face softens a later claim. A shared task makes a later request feel less like an outside demand. A charged image can make a risk feel huge. None of these cues replaces substance. They change the conditions in which substance is judged.

A good setup earns attention for the right reason. If a tenant needs to see the broken stair before voting on repairs, take the meeting to the stairwell. If a patient is scared by a machine, name the fear before explaining the scan. If a donor needs to remember why the program matters, put the student's work in front of her before the gift amount. The cue should help the person see more clearly.

You can spot the bad version by the aftertaste it leaves. The person says yes fast, then later feels steered. The room applauds, then cannot explain the choice. The customer signs, then calls back confused. Those are signs that the setup was stronger than the case. A sound setup makes the later facts easier to face, not harder to inspect.

Hand the listener a better first frame. Show the actual crack before the repair quote. Move the talk out of the hallway if the hallway cues fear. Ask people to sort one card together before asking them to own the plan. Small changes like these work because they meet the mind before it has settled on what matters.

There is a limit, and it matters in daily work. A setup becomes suspect when it hides cost, fakes urgency, borrows trust that was not earned, or makes a person choose while too stirred up to think. The same method can clarify or cloud. The difference is whether the person would still thank you for the setup after seeing the full facts.

At the end, keep the move modest. You are not trying to win by mood alone. You are trying to give the real issue a fair first place in the person's mind. If the first cue is true, relevant, and kind to the choice in front of them, use it. If it only makes the yes easier for you, take it out.

Before the next important ask, do a thirty-second audit. What will they see first? What feeling will that create? What comparison will be active? What identity will be touched? Then change one thing so the first cue serves the real decision. Use the setup to help people see the real choice, not to hide it.

examples.title: Vera clips the half-filled scorecard to each trainee's lanyard

planSpec.audience: a trainer using unfinished progress ethically
planSpec.stakes: whether the setup helps the person judge the choice clearly or tilts the moment in a misleading way

examples.scenario: Vera clips a half-filled scorecard to each trainee's lanyard at 9:22 a.m. in room 4C. The new support reps have ignored the quality rubric for two days. Each card shows two completed skills and one blank box labeled calm close. The blank space keeps drawing their eyes. Vera must decide whether to use that pull for practice or turn it into a public ranking board.
examples.whatToDo: Keep the open loop private and skill-based. Ask each trainee to complete the blank box with one recorded call by lunch.
examples.whyItMatters: Unfinished progress holds attention because people want closure. It supports learning when it points to the next action, not to public shame.

examples.title: Niko leaves one puzzle piece missing from the museum case

planSpec.audience: a docent using mystery to hold attention
planSpec.stakes: whether the setup helps the person judge the choice clearly or tilts the moment in a misleading way
planSpec.requiredBeat: Sunday 11:09 a.m. in the fossils gallery

examples.scenario: Niko leaves one puzzle piece missing from the museum case at 11:09 a.m. in the fossils gallery. Children press their noses toward the glass, searching the empty outline beside the trilobite. The label does not start with facts. It asks what part of the animal would fit the gap. Niko has to decide when to reveal the answer as parents stay by the case, pointing at ridges.
examples.whatToDo: Use the missing piece to invite prediction, then reveal the answer after visitors have looked closely.
examples.whyItMatters: A gap creates a small itch to know. The facts that follow land better because the eyes have already worked for them.

examples.title: Amadou writes the customer's initials on the repair tag

planSpec.audience: a dispatcher making a status update self-relevant
planSpec.stakes: whether the setup helps the person judge the choice clearly or tilts the moment in a misleading way
planSpec.requiredBeat: Tuesday 4:48 p.m. at the dispatch counter

examples.scenario: Amadou writes the customer's initials on the repair tag at 4:48 p.m. while the dryer parts list prints. "Another delay?" Mrs. Havel asks through the phone. He must decide whether to recite the queue or make the next step hers. "Your tag, H.R., is the one I am moving to tomorrow's first truck," he says. The initials feel less like a system and more like a promise.
examples.whatToDo: Make the next step visibly tied to her case, then give the exact truck window. Avoid vague queue language.
examples.whyItMatters: Self-relevance holds attention because the person can see herself in the process. A named tag beats a general reassurance.

examples.title: Claudia covers the final number on the budget slide

planSpec.audience: a treasurer using mystery before a budget decision
planSpec.stakes: whether the setup helps the person judge the choice clearly or tilts the moment in a misleading way
planSpec.requiredBeat: Wednesday 7:15 p.m. in the library meeting room

examples.scenario: Claudia covers the final number on the budget slide at 7:15 p.m. in the library meeting room. Board members predict the summer reading gap is under 4,000 dollars. She reveals the uncovered total: 17,860. Chairs creak. The mystery held them through the line items they usually skim. Claudia must decide whether to use the surprise to rush a vote or slow down for questions.
examples.whatToDo: Use the reveal to earn careful attention, then walk through the tradeoffs. Do not turn surprise into pressure.
examples.whyItMatters: Mystery can make people care enough to listen. It becomes manipulation when the reveal is used to outrun scrutiny.

examples.title: Hiro finds the unopened envelope under the gym scoreboard

planSpec.audience: a coach seeing an open loop misfire
planSpec.stakes: whether the setup helps the person judge the choice clearly or tilts the moment in a misleading way

examples.scenario: Hiro finds the unopened envelope under the gym scoreboard at 8:36 p.m. after practice. He had written each player's shooting goal inside and told them not to open it until playoffs. Three envelopes are missing, six are untouched, and nobody remembers the drill. The mystery lasted one day because it never connected to practice. Hiro has to decide what kind of open loop belongs on tomorrow's court.
examples.whatToDo: Make the gap visible during practice: one blank shot chart per player, filled after each drill. Tie closure to the behavior you want.
examples.whyItMatters: A secret envelope is only curiosity. A visible incomplete chart keeps attention on the next rep.

examples.title: Parisa changes the app tour from features to the user's unfinished setup

planSpec.audience: a product manager holding attention through personal completion
planSpec.stakes: whether the setup helps the person judge the choice clearly or tilts the moment in a misleading way
planSpec.requiredBeat: Friday 2:02 p.m. in a usability lab

examples.scenario: Before 2:02 p.m., Parisa's app tour showed seven polished feature cards and users skipped them. After she changed the first screen to Your desk is 40 percent set up, testers stayed to connect calendars, folders, and alerts. One tester tapped the progress ring twice, frowning at the missing slice. Parisa must decide how much unfinished progress is helpful.
examples.whatToDo: Show only the setup steps that matter for first value, and let the user finish them quickly. Keep the progress ring honest.
examples.whyItMatters: Personal completion holds attention because the open loop belongs to the user. Too many steps turn the loop into a trap.

questions.prompt: A manager is about to ask a tired team to adopt a new process after a messy outage, and the first thing on the screen is a dense policy page. What should happen first if the goal is to use self-relevance, unfinished gaps, and mystery hold attention after they catch it without clouding judgment?
choices: Change the first cue so it supports the real decision, then make the request in plain words.
Add more facts immediately and trust the listener to sort the setup out later.
Use the strongest emotional cue available, even if it is only loosely connected to the choice.
questions.explanation: The best answer adjusts the cue before the ask while keeping the real choice visible. It uses give people a meaningful open loop they want to close, instead of adding pressure or piling on facts too late.

reviewCards.front: You are about to make a request. What should you inspect before the first sentence?
reviewCards.back: Inspect the first cue: what the listener will see, feel, compare, or identify with before the ask. Change it if it pulls attention away from the real choice.

reviewCards.front: A cue gets attention but also makes the choice feel rushed. What is the repair?
reviewCards.back: Keep only cues that help people judge well. Slow the moment down, add missing facts, or move the cue out of first position if it creates pressure without clarity.

reviewCards.front: A team agrees in the room, then forgets by tomorrow. What did the setup miss?
reviewCards.back: The yes needed an after-cue: a visible next step, a calendar hold, a shared note, or a first action before the room broke apart.

reviewCards.front: When does a strong setup become unethical?
reviewCards.back: It crosses the line when it hides cost, fakes urgency, borrows trust, or makes a weaker offer feel stronger than the facts support.

implementationPlan.coreSkill: The core skill is setup judgment. Before you ask, choose the cue, place, timing, or shared action that helps the other person see the real choice clearly.

ifThenPlans.plan: If I need a decision at work, then I will check what the room sees first and move one object, slide, or number so it supports give people a meaningful open loop they want to close.
If a health choice is coming, then I will remove cues that create panic and put the most relevant evidence where the person can see it before deciding.
If I am making a personal ask, then I will start with shared purpose and one concrete object instead of old frustration or vague pressure.
If someone says yes to a change, then I will help set the first cue for follow-through before we leave the conversation.

implementationPlan.twentyFourHourChallenge: Within the next 24 hours, choose one real ask and write down the first thing the other person will see, hear, or compare. Change one cue so the setup helps them judge the choice fairly.
implementationPlan.weeklyPractice: Once this week, review one request that worked or failed. Separate the ask from the setup, then name the cue that shaped the result most.
